summary:
NISAR Change Explorer is a web app that turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar images into plain answers anyone can understand. Floods usually come with thick cloud, and often happen at night, so ordinary satellite photos see nothing. NISAR’s radar sees through both, but its data is huge and made for scientists.

Our app does the hard part. You pick a place, and it finds the right NISAR images and compares the radar from before and after the event. It then maps where water appeared or went away, and explains the result in everyday language. It also suggests the likely cause using rainfall, land and fire data, and checks the result against NASA’s OPERA water maps. It says honestly how sure it can be; wet farmland, for example, can look like water.

This addresses the challenge by making NISAR’s “dance” of radar signals readable for people who aren’t experts. It matters because rescue teams, reporters, farmers and families need to know where the water went, even when the sky is covered. The app is free, open source, and runs any place on Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works

NISAR Change Explorer turns NISAR radar data into a simple answer to one question: what changed here? You choose a place on a 3D globe or open a ready-made flood story, and the app does the rest:

  1. Finds the data. It searches NASA Earthdata for NISAR images (Level-2 GCOV) from before and after the event.
  2. Gets only your area. It reads just the part of each large radar file that covers your area, over the internet, and saves it so it isn't downloaded twice. It shows the download progress and the time left.
  3. Cleans the radar. It reduces speckle noise and combines several passes into one steady "before" picture and one "after" picture.
  4. Finds water. Calm water reflects radar away from the satellite, so it looks dark in both radar channels (HH and HV). The app marks water that appears after the event, ignores water that was already there, and keeps only changes that show up in more than one later pass.
  5. Explains it. It shows the change on a map with charts, writes a plain-words summary, suggests a likely cause using rainfall, elevation and fire data, and compares its water map with NASA's OPERA water maps.
  6. Answers common questions, but only the ones it can answer from that place's data.

Benefits

  • It works through cloud, at night and in the rain, when ordinary satellite photos are useless.
  • There's no jargon and no need for GIS or radar skills.
  • It's honest about what it doesn't know. For example, it warns that wet farmland can look like water.
  • You can follow places and get alerts when new satellite data arrives.
  • It's free and open source.

Intended impact

  • Rescue and relief teams see where water spread, so they know where to go first.
  • Reporters can check flood claims against satellite evidence.
  • Farmers and families can see what happened to their land.

More broadly, it makes a new NASA–ISRO mission useful to the public, not just to scientists.

Tools and technology

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI and Uvicorn, with h5py and fsspec for reading NISAR HDF5 files over the internet, and NumPy and SciPy for the radar processing.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with MapLibre GL for the 3D globe and maps, and Chart.js for the charts.
  • Data: NASA–ISRO NISAR GCOV through NASA Earthdata, and NASA OPERA water maps for comparison, plus rainfall, elevation and fire data.
  • Hosting and tools: GitHub, and Vercel for the online demo. The full app runs on a laptop.
  • AI use: Claude (Anthropic) helped with code, documentation, the demo video and its voice-over. The video carries an AI notice.

What makes it creative

  • It turns radar into a story: a plain answer, a likely cause, and an honest note on how sure it is, rather than just a map of pixels.
  • The flood stories let anyone explore real events in seconds.
  • It checks its own work against another NASA product and says so openly when the two don't agree.
  • It downloads only what it needs from very large files and shows clearly how long that will take.

What our team considered

  • Accuracy and honesty. We tested against OPERA maps, logged the experiments that failed, and kept the confidence levels conservative.
  • Ease of use. We wrote plain language, avoided technical terms, and tested on both laptop and phone.
  • Speed. We download only the area needed, cache it, and the online demo opens instantly.
  • Security. No login details are stored in the code or on the public demo.
  • Data rules. We credit every data source and use no NASA logos.
  • Limits of free hosting. The online demo shows real prepared results, and the full app runs any place locally.
